studies.title: Finding out if good sleep makes us kinder
studies.sub: Rate your sleep, then split $10 with a stranger in a quick sharing game. Your choices show whether well-rested people really give more — and whether better rest could nudge everyday kindness.
studies.abstract: Recruiting observational behavioural study (NCT07697092). Goal: test whether sleep quality, sleep timing and chronotype are associated with prosocial allocation decisions. Participants complete the Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index and Munich Chronotype Questionnaire plus a brief Dictator-game allocation task. We need your sleep self-report and sharing choices to link rest to generosity.

studies.title: Better diets for healthier ageing
studies.sub: Log a typical day of eating — no judgment. Your honest diary joins a 171,000-person cohort, turning everyday food into real evidence on how diet shapes long-term health.
studies.abstract: Recruiting web-based cohort (NCT03335644, NutriNet-Santé). Goal: investigate the complex link between nutrition and health status via detailed dietary assessment. We need your real dietary intake to relate eating patterns to long-term health outcomes.

studies.title: Pinning down the foods that trigger IBS
studies.sub: Tell us what you eat and how your gut reacts. Your answers calibrate a simple food questionnaire against real IBS symptoms — a tool doctors could use to pin down triggers.
studies.abstract: Recruiting validation study (NCT05293769). Goal: validate a food frequency questionnaire (incl. FODMAPs) across populations and relate intake to IBS symptoms and self-assessed physical activity. We need your diet + symptom reports to test the questionnaire's reliability.

studies.title: Care that fits the real days of fibromyalgia
studies.sub: Rate today's pain, fatigue and limits. Your daily ratings reveal the swings that averages hide, helping design fibromyalgia care that fits real days, not textbook ones.
studies.abstract: Recruiting observational study (NCT07826520). Goal: examine whether daily changes in pain and fatigue relate to functional impact in adults with fibromyalgia. We need repeated daily symptom ratings to capture fluctuations that average scores miss.

studies.title: Support that answers early-pregnancy worries
studies.sub: Share what worries you and where you look for answers. Your concerns shape what a new pregnancy app actually helps with — support built around real first-trimester questions.
studies.abstract: Recruiting study (NCT07114471). Goal: address pregnant women's first-trimester worries and information needs with mHealth solutions. We need your real worries and information gaps to design support that actually helps.

studies.title: Mental-health screening for kids with heart defects
studies.sub: Answer as a parent or young person about mood and daily life. Your responses test whether an online check-in can catch mental-health struggles that clinic visits miss.
studies.abstract: Recruiting feasibility study (NCT05709470, Mind the Heart). Goal: document feasibility of an online parent/child screening model for mental disorders in children/adolescents with congenital heart disease. We need parent/child screening responses to validate the model.

studies.title: Spotting when stress steers disease
studies.sub: Rate your mood, worry and sleep. Your answers feed a cohort tracking how chronic stress steers illness — helping doctors see when to step in earlier.
studies.abstract: Recruiting prospective cohort (NCT07529626, MIND-PANC). Goal: explore associations of chronic psychological stress with disease progression and outcomes. Participants complete mood, worry and sleep questionnaires at baseline and follow-up. We need your stress self-report to link mind and body.

studies.title: Predicting runners' injuries before they happen
studies.sub: Share your training, sleep and life stress. Your answers build a model that predicts who gets injured — sparing runners months on the sidelines.
studies.authors: National Yang Ming Chiao Tung University
studies.abstract: Recruiting study (NCT07929311). Goal: develop a biopsychosocial prediction model for running-related injuries. We need your training load, stress, sleep and recovery data to predict who gets injured.

studies.title: Weakening the grip of group pressure
studies.sub: See the group's answer, then give your own. Your choices measure how often we cave to a wrong majority — and what helps us stand firm.
studies.abstract: Replication of Asch's conformity experiments (1951). Goal: measure how group pressure shifts individual judgement on clear tasks. We need your independent judgement vs the group's to quantify conformity.

studies.title: Mapping the moral wiring behind hard choices
studies.sub: Make the calls in two classic dilemmas and say why. Your choices reveal whether emotion or calculation drives your ethics, mapping the moral wiring we all share.
studies.authors: Joshua Greene et al. (2001), Harvard University
studies.abstract: Based on Greene's fMRI moral-judgment study (2001). Goal: distinguish emotional/personal from impersonal/cost-benefit moral reasoning. We need your dilemma choices to map the emotional vs calculative divide.

studies.title: Learning what keeps groups cooperating
studies.sub: Decide how much to contribute and whether to punish cheaters at your own cost. Your decisions show what actually keeps groups cooperating.
studies.authors: Ernst Fehr & Simon Gächter (2000), University of Zurich
studies.abstract: Based on Fehr & Gächter's public-goods experiments (2000). Goal: test altruistic punishment and cooperation. We need your contribution and punishment choices to measure how cooperation is sustained.

studies.title: Better lie detection than gut feeling
studies.sub: Judge which of two accounts is truthful and name the cues you trusted. Your verdicts reveal what really gives a liar away — beyond the gut feeling most of us rely on.
studies.abstract: Based on Vrij's deception-detection research (2008). Goal: identify which verbal/non-verbal cues people use to detect lies, and how accurate they are. We need your truth/lie judgements and the cues you used.

studies.title: Fairer verdicts from how jurors really decide
studies.sub: Weigh the evidence, deliver a verdict and say what would change your mind. Your reasoning shows how jurors actually decide — and where justice can go wrong.
studies.authors: Harry Kalven & Hans Zeisel (1966), University of Chicago
studies.abstract: Based on Kalven & Zeisel's The American Jury (1966). Goal: understand how jurors weigh evidence and reach verdicts. We need your verdict and reasoning to study decision patterns.

studies.title: A personality profile science can rely on
studies.sub: Rate yourself honestly on a few everyday habits. Your answers build a Big Five trait profile on the standard model used across psychology research.
studies.abstract: Based on the NEO five-factor inventory (Costa & McCrae, 1992). Goal: measure openness, conscientiousness, extraversion, agreeableness, neuroticism. We need your self-ratings to build your trait profile.

studies.title: Catching depression earlier
studies.sub: Rate your last two weeks on the PHQ-9, the screen clinics actually use. Your answers score your mood and help validate faster ways to catch depression early. Not a diagnosis.
studies.authors: Kurt Kroenke et al. (2001), Indiana University
studies.abstract: The PHQ-9 (Kroenke, Spitzer & Williams, 2001) — a validated 9-item depression screen. Goal: measure depressive symptom severity over the last 2 weeks. We need your responses to score mood. (Not a diagnosis.)

studies.title: Spotting anxiety before it takes over
studies.sub: Rate the last two weeks on the GAD-7, the check clinicians rely on. Your answers score your worry and help refine a tool that gets people support sooner. Not a diagnosis.
studies.authors: Robert Spitzer et al. (2006), Columbia University
studies.abstract: The GAD-7 (Spitzer, Kroenke, Williams & Löwe, 2006) — a validated 7-item anxiety screen. Goal: measure generalised anxiety severity over the last 2 weeks. We need your responses to score anxiety. (Not a diagnosis.)

studies.title: Finding out what really restores good sleep
studies.sub: Tell us about your nights and days on the gold-standard sleep index. Your answers score your sleep and help research what really restores it.
studies.authors: Daniel Buysse et al. (1989), University of Pittsburgh
studies.abstract: The PSQI (Buysse et al., 1989) — a validated sleep-quality index. Goal: measure sleep quality and disturbances over a month. We need your sleep self-report to compute your PSQI score.

studies.title: Schedules that fit every body clock
studies.sub: Share when you naturally rise and peak. Your answers place your body clock on the morning–evening scale, helping design work and school schedules that fit real biology.
studies.authors: Jim Horne & Olov Östberg (1976), Loughborough University
studies.abstract: The Morningness–Eveningness Questionnaire (Horne & Östberg, 1976). Goal: classify chronotype. We need your timing preferences to score your body clock.

studies.title: Understanding why good people disagree
studies.sub: Rate what matters to you on the Moral Foundations Questionnaire. Your answers map your moral 'taste buds' and help explain divides that facts alone can't.
studies.abstract: The Moral Foundations Questionnaire (Haidt & Graham, 2011). Goal: measure care, fairness, loyalty, authority, sanctity foundations. We need your ratings to build your moral profile.

studies.title: Measuring the stress that harms health
studies.sub: Rate your month on the most-used stress scale in research. Your answers score how controllable life feels and link it to health outcomes.
studies.authors: Sheldon Cohen et al. (1983), Carnegie Mellon University
studies.abstract: The Perceived Stress Scale (Cohen, Kamarck & Mermelstein, 1983). Goal: measure how unpredictable/uncontrollable life feels. We need your responses to score perceived stress.

studies.title: Spotting loneliness before it takes a toll
studies.sub: Rate how connected you feel on the UCLA scale. Your answers help research spot isolation early — loneliness harms health as much as smoking, yet stays invisible.
studies.abstract: The UCLA Loneliness Scale v3 (Russell, 1996). Goal: measure subjective loneliness/social isolation. We need your responses to score connection.

studies.title: Finding what actually makes life feel good
studies.sub: Rate your life as a whole on the global standard for wellbeing. Your answers feed decades of research on what actually makes people thrive.
studies.authors: Ed Diener et al. (1985), University of Illinois
studies.abstract: The Satisfaction With Life Scale (Diener et al., 1985). Goal: measure global life satisfaction. We need your ratings to score wellbeing.

studies.title: Understanding where self-worth comes from
studies.sub: Rate how you see yourself on the classic self-esteem scale. Your honest answers help research understand where self-worth comes from — and how to protect it.
studies.abstract: The Rosenberg Self-Esteem Scale (1965). Goal: measure global self-worth. We need your responses to score self-esteem.

studies.title: Uncovering the biases we don't endorse
studies.sub: Make quick pairings and reflect on them. Your responses reveal automatic associations you may not endorse — the biases research is learning to undo.
studies.authors: Anthony Greenwald et al. (1998), University of Washington
studies.abstract: The Implicit Association Test (Greenwald, McGhee & Schwartz, 1998). Goal: measure automatic associations between concepts. We need your pairing responses to compute implicit bias scores.

studies.title: Protecting justice from malleable memory
studies.sub: Read the scenario and report what you recall. Your answers measure how suggestion reshapes memory — with real stakes for eyewitness justice.
studies.authors: Elizabeth Loftus & Jacqueline Pickrell (1995), UC Irvine
studies.abstract: Based on Loftus & Pickrell's 'lost in the mall' false-memory study (1995). Goal: test whether suggested events can be implanted as memories. We need your recall to measure suggestibility.

studies.title: How stories quietly change our minds
studies.sub: Rate how stories pull you in. Your answers show when fiction quietly reshapes real-world beliefs — and when it doesn't.
studies.authors: Melanie Green & Timothy Brock (2000), University at Buffalo
studies.abstract: The Narrative Transportation Scale (Green & Brock, 2000). Goal: measure immersion in stories and its persuasive effect. We need your responses to score transportation.

studies.title: Telling self-interest from darker traits
studies.sub: Rate yourself honestly on the Dark Triad measure. Your answers help research tell ordinary self-interest from something darker.
studies.abstract: The Short Dark Triad (Paulhus & Williams, 2014). Goal: measure subclinical dark traits. We need your honest self-ratings.

studies.title: Reaching every kind of thinker
studies.sub: Rate how you like to think. Your answers help research understand who digs deep into hard problems — and how to reach everyone else.
studies.authors: John Cacioppo & Richard Petty (1982), University of Chicago
studies.abstract: The Need for Cognition Scale (Cacioppo & Petty, 1982). Goal: measure enjoyment of effortful cognitive activity. We need your responses to score NFC.

studies.title: Designing tech we can put down
studies.sub: Rate your phone habits honestly. Your answers score problematic use and help design tech we can actually put down.
studies.authors: Min Kwon et al. (2013), Chungnam National University
studies.abstract: The Smartphone Addiction Scale–Short Version (Kwon et al., 2013). Goal: measure problematic smartphone use. We need your responses to score addiction risk.

studies.title: Defusing the risks of chronic boredom
studies.sub: Rate your restlessness. Your answers help research understand a feeling that quietly predicts risk-taking, dropout and poor health.
studies.authors: Richard Farmer & Norman Sundberg (1992), Oregon Research Institute
studies.abstract: The Boredom Proneness Scale (Farmer & Sundberg, 1992). Goal: measure trait boredom. We need your responses to score boredom proneness.

studies.title: Sharpening attention against distraction
studies.sub: Name the ink, not the word. Your responses reveal how attention fights automatic reading — a cornerstone of cognitive research.
studies.authors: J. Ridley Stroop (1935), George Peabody College
studies.abstract: The Stroop task (1935). Goal: measure interference between reading and colour-naming (selective attention). We need your responses to measure the Stroop interference effect.

studies.title: Finding where obedience should stop
studies.sub: Say what you'd do and why when an order clashes with your conscience. Your answers map the boundaries of obedience — without any real harm.
studies.abstract: Based on Milgram's obedience study (1963). Goal: measure willingness to obey authority against personal conscience. We need your judgement responses (no real harm involved).

studies.title: Protecting memory and thinking
studies.sub: Thinking and memory change across life. Tell us about your memory, focus and mental clarity. Your answers help ways to protect cognitive health. It's a short, confidential questionnaire.
studies.authors: The University of Hong Kong (2026). ClinicalTrials.gov NCT07822828.
studies.abstract: Thinking and memory change across life. This recruiting study (interventional) asks participants about your memory, focus and mental clarity. Participation is a short online questionnaire; responses contribute to ways to protect cognitive health. Source: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT07822828 (The University of Hong Kong). Not a diagnostic tool.
